40 Which particle is a fundamental particle?
A
electron
B
hadron
C
neutron
D
proton

hints: Notice the wording fundamental particle means a particle with no smaller constituents, not just a small particle like proton or neutron.
Connect hadron, proton and neutron to the quark model - hadrons are made of quarks, and protons and neutrons each contain three quarks.
Recall the electron belongs to the lepton group, which like quarks has no quark substructure.
walkthrough: Start from the definition: a fundamental particle cannot be split into smaller particles made of quarks.
Recall that a hadron is any particle made of quarks, including baryons made of three quarks and mesons made of a quark and antiquark.
Apply this to the proton with quark content $uud$ and the neutron with quark content $udd$ - both are baryons and therefore hadrons with internal structure.
Recall that the electron is a lepton, one of the six leptons that are not made of quarks and have no known substructure.
Therefore only the electron in this list satisfies the definition of fundamental. This is option A

A.explanation: The electron is a lepton with no internal quark structure and is treated as fundamental in the Standard Model.

B.explanation: A hadron is a family of particles made of quarks, so by definition it is not fundamental.

C.explanation: A neutron is a baryon made of three quarks, $udd$, so it has internal structure.

D.explanation: A proton is a baryon made of three quarks, $uud$, so it has internal structure.
